title: Differentiating nonfluent/agrammatic and logopenic primary progressive aphasia in Catalan-Spanish bilinguals by applying multilingual multimodal machine learning to connected speech
authors: Pugalenthi, L. S.; Collins, A. P.; Colomer, N. M.; Marques-Kiderle, S.-K.; Wagner Rodriguez, C. A.; Chaires, J. C. H.; Motta, W. A.; Filella-Merce, J.; Li, J. J.; Llanos, F.; Zhu, N.; Rubio-Guerra, S.; Illan-Gala, I.; Borrego-Ecija, S.; Llado, A.; Fortea, J.; Lleo, A.; Sanchez-Valle, R.; Henry, M. L.; Santos, M. A. S.; Grasso, S. M.
abstract: BackgroundThe nonfluent/agrammatic (nfv) and logopenic (lv) variants of primary progressive aphasia (PPA) disrupt fluency through distinct underlying neurocognitive mechanisms. Differential diagnosis currently requires hours of cognitive-linguistic testing, with additional barriers for bilingual patients due to a shortage of bilingual service providers and a lack of well-established assessment methods. In English speakers, a promising automated approach for differentiating nfvPPA and lvPPA is to derive speech-timing measures and linguistic features from connected speech as input to machine learning (ML) classification algorithms. To our knowledge, this approach has not been evaluated in the context of bilingualism. MethodsThirty-four Catalan-Spanish simultaneous bilingual patients (lv = 24, nfv = 10) were asked to describe a picture (Western Aphasia Battery Picnic Scene) in both their dominant and non- dominant language. From the participants recorded response, we derived four feature sets: speech-timing measures, derived with PRAAT; word-level parameters, derived from corpora; linguistic features, derived with the natural language processing tools SpaCy and CLAN; image-text congruence scores, derived with the vision-language encoder Multilingual-CLIP. Each feature set was fed into classification algorithms for differentiating nfv from lv in participants non-dominant and dominant samples. Then, we combined each feature sets classifier into an ensemble model. We used the McNemar test to determine the statistical significance of differences in classification performance between responses in the non-dominant and dominant language. ResultsThe best-performing classifier achieved F1 macro scores of 93% (word-level parameters) and 92% (ensemble) in the non-dominant and dominant language, respectively. For all feature sets and ensemble models, classification performance did not significantly differ between the non-dominant and dominant language. Ensemble modeling did not significantly improve classification performance in either language. ConclusionsTaking advantage of recent advances in multilingual multimodal machine learning, we accurately differentiate Spanish-Catalan bilingual individuals with nfvPPA and lvPPA using a largely automated, time-efficient (1-2 minutes), and ecologically valid connected-speech-based approach. Future directions include evaluating this approach on larger datasets balanced by PPA subtype, using automated transcriptions of connected speech. Our study represents a step towards addressing current inequities in PPA differential diagnosis for non-English-speaking bilingual speakers. Trial registrationData from the clinical trial NCT05741853 was retrospectively analyzed

infographic.key_insight: Multilingual multimodal machine learning can accurately distinguish nonfluent/agrammatic from logopenic primary progressive aphasia in Catalan-Spanish bilinguals using connected speech.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help speed up and standardize differential diagnosis for bilingual patients when language-specific expert assessment is limited.
method: 34 Catalan-Spanish simultaneous bilingual patients were recorded describing a picture in both dominant and non-dominant languages.
Four feature sets were extracted from speech: timing, word-level, linguistic, and image-text congruence features.
Multiple classifiers and an ensemble model were tested to separate nfvPPA from lvPPA.
infographic.evidence_signal: In this 34-patient study, the best model reached 93% macro-F1 in the non-dominant language and 92% in the dominant language, with no significant performance difference between languages.
infographic.watch_item: Small sample size and single-prompt, bilingual-specific testing may limit generalizability and require external validation before routine use.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiating nonfluent/agrammatic and logopenic primary progressive aphasia in Catalan-Spanish bilinguals by applying multilingual multimodal machine learning to connected speech

title: Multi-omics approach to map a clinically diverse large cohort with homozygous founder RAG1 p.C176F variant among Old Order Mennonites
authors: Potts, E.; Toth, M.; Brigatti, K. W.; Puffenberger, E. G.; Suhet, P. R.; Talib, M.; Koehler, A. E.; Gaal, Z.; Larsen, K. A.; Miller, R. Z.; Gibson, D. J.; Mendez, P.; An, Z.; Bednarski, J. J.; Blazso, P.; Bosticardo, M.; Chandra, S.; Chinn, I. K.; Clark, J. W.; Condino-Neto, A.; Delmonte, O. M.; Dimitrova, D.; Edwards, E. S. J.; Halade, G. V.; Heimall, J. R.; Hendel, A.; Henrickson, S. E.; Herman, K. E.; Joshi, A.; Kenney, H.; Kitcharoensakkul, M.; Magro, G.; Martin, E. C.; Oliveira-Junior, E. B.; Ong, M.-S.; Ospina, O. E.; Pala, F.; Palmer, K.; Raasch, J. P.; Salamon, M.; Scharer, C. D.; Sero
abstract: Partially preserved function of recombination-activating genes (RAG) 1 and 2 can be linked to divergent and hard-to-predict clinical and immunological phenotypes, even among close relatives. It is unclear how intrinsic RAG hypomorphism interacts with extrinsic environmental pressures to shape clinical trajectory. We dissect this phenomenon in a unique cohort of 18 Old Order Mennonite individuals with a novel missense founder RAG1 variant (p.C176F) with 25.8% recombinase activity of wild-type protein. After studying a myriad of markers, we demonstrate varying severity and progression of clinical disease (predominantly in females) that paralleled decline in CMV-specific immune competence, break in tolerance with hallmark presence of antibodies to IFN, a TH1/IFN{gamma}-driven inflammatory milieu with elevated serum markers (CXCL9/10), expansion of follicular helper T cells and clonal B cells enriched for autoreactive-prone VH4.34 B cell receptor. BCR and TCR repertoires carry the fingerprints of both extrinsic and RAG-driven intrinsic changes. Through this experiment of nature, our cohort demonstrated that partial RAG deficiency (pRD) is not a monolithic disease but the result of compounded RAG intrinsic and extrinsic events. Overall, this study uses multi-omics approaches to dissect the contribution of a hypomorphic RAG variant to variable severity of clinical disease and immunological dysregulation at cellular and molecular level. Emerging biomarkers of a multi-omic roadmap should allow monitoring of progression of clinical disease and guide who and when to treat with hematopoietic stem cell transplant in pRD. One sentence summaryA unique cohort of pediatric and adult US Mennonite patients with shared novel partial RAG defect and variable penetrance of disease allow correlation of clinical severity with RAG-intrinsic and extrinsic factors driving plasticity in T and B cell competence to eliminate infections and tolerance to self.

infographic.key_insight: A hypomorphic founder RAG1 variant caused highly variable immune disease, showing that partial RAG deficiency is shaped by both inherited defect strength and external immune pressures.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The multi-omic biomarkers described may help stratify which patients with partial RAG deficiency are progressing and could benefit from closer monitoring or hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
method: Studied 18 Old Order Mennonite individuals with the RAG1 p.C176F founder variant
Combined multi-omics, immune phenotyping, and repertoire analysis of BCR/TCR
Measured recombinase activity, cytokine/chemokine markers, autoantibodies, and CMV-specific immunity
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a clinically diverse cohort with the variant showing 25.8% wild-type recombinase activity and linked immune signatures across cellular and molecular readouts.
infographic.watch_item: Findings come from a rare, genetically enriched cohort, so the biomarkers and severity patterns may not generalize broadly without external validation.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-omics approach to map a clinically diverse large cohort with homozygous founder RAG1 p.C176F variant among Old Order Mennonites

title: Comparison of Facial Feature Grading by an AI-Based System Versus Human Expert Grading on Images Under Standardized Clinical and At-Home Settings
authors: Danko, D.; Tlyachev, T.; Kiselev, K.; Bousseksou, L.; Camel, E.; Stamatas, G.; Georgievskaya, A.
abstract: Digital photography remains the gold standard for dermatological assessment, but reliance on standardized stationary image-capture systems limits trial scalability, whereas smartphones combined with computer vision artificial intelligence (AI) could enable hybrid and decentralized clinical trials (DCTs). This study assessed the facial feature grading of an AI-based system against expert panel consensus across three settings with decreasing acquisition control: Standard Studio Imaging (SSI), Clinic Smartphone Imaging (CSI), and Home Smartphone Imaging (HSI). Expert inter-rater reliability was good to excellent (median ICC 0.84-0.90), and the system showed high operator-independent test-retest repeatability across independently captured images (median ICC 0.97-0.98). Agreement with experts was maintained across all settings for macro-geometric features (ptosis{rho} = 0.74-0.81, nasolabial fold{rho} = 0.68-0.79) and for discrete pigmentation and inflammatory lesions (pigmented spot density{rho} = 0.62-0.76), declined for fine-texture features under uncontrolled acquisition (forehead wrinkles{rho} = 0.76 to 0.48), and remained limited for color-dependent features irrespective of setting. These findings support the AI-based system as an objective grading tool for a defined subset of facial endpoints in hybrid and DCTs in dermatology.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-based facial grading system closely matched expert ratings for several structural and lesion-related facial features, especially in more controlled image settings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could make dermatology assessments more scalable in hybrid and decentralized trials by enabling consistent smartphone-based image grading.
method: Compared AI grading with expert panel consensus across standardized studio, clinic smartphone, and home smartphone image settings.
Evaluated repeatability across independently captured images and agreement on multiple facial feature types.
Tested performance on macro-geometric, pigmentation, inflammatory, fine-texture, and color-dependent endpoints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Expert inter-rater reliability was good to excellent (median ICC 0.84–0.90), and the AI showed very high test-retest repeatability (median ICC 0.97–0.98) with strongest agreement for macro-geometric and some lesion features.
infographic.watch_item: Performance dropped for fine-texture features under less controlled acquisition, and color-dependent features remained limited across settings.
infographic.paper_title: Comparison of Facial Feature Grading by an AI-Based System Versus Human Expert Grading on Images Under Standardized Clinical and At-Home Settings

title: Improving MASLD Identification in Patients with T2D: A Computable Phenotype Framework Integrating Structured Data and Clinical Notes
authors: Chen, Y.; Sharma, A.; Yang, Q.; Chen, Y.; Yin, R.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is highly prevalent among individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D), yet accurate identification from electronic health records (EHRs) remains challenging because clinically relevant information is fragmented across structured data and unstructured clinical documentation. We developed a rule-based computable phenotype (CP) framework that integrates structured EHRs with clinical notes for scalable MASLD identification in patients with T2D. The framework comprises five complementary CP algorithms derived from validated fibrosis indices and liver injury biomarkers, together with a lightweight natural language processing module that identifies MASLD-related evidence using keyword matching, contextual filtering, and negation detection. The proposed framework was systematically evaluated across multiple threshold settings, with additional validation through age- and sex-stratified analyses and manual chart review. The findings demonstrate that integrating structured and unstructured EHR data provides an accurate and scalable framework for real-world MASLD phenotyping and offers a practical strategy for developing CPs for other chronic diseases.

infographic.key_insight: A rule-based computable phenotype that combines structured EHR data with clinical notes can improve MASLD identification in patients with type 2 diabetes.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better phenotyping could help researchers and health systems more reliably find MASLD cases in T2D populations for screening, cohort building, and outcomes studies.
method: Built five complementary phenotype algorithms using fibrosis indices and liver injury biomarkers.
Added lightweight NLP to detect MASLD mentions in clinical notes with keyword matching, context filtering, and negation detection.
Evaluated performance across multiple thresholds and validated findings with age/sex-stratified analyses and manual chart review.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports systematic evaluation across threshold settings plus manual chart review and stratified analyses, supporting real-world feasibility and accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on note quality, site-specific documentation patterns, and the portability of rule-based thresholds across health systems.
infographic.paper_title: Improving MASLD Identification in Patients with T2D: A Computable Phenotype Framework Integrating Structured Data and Clinical Notes

title: Biomarker Convert: a novel approach to transform plasma pTau217 results across immunoassay and mass spectrometry analytical platforms
authors: Quadrini, K. J.; Aubrecht, J.; Vernhes, F.; Zeng, X.; Johnson, A. D.; Snitz, B. E.; Cohen, A. D.; Tooker, R.; Quiceno, M. E.; Campbell, B. M.; Karikari, T. K.; Swanson, C. J.
abstract: INTRODUCTIONWe report the development and validation of a novel computational tool to cross-convert plasma pTau217 results from different assays to facilitate recruitment for therapeutic trials and observational studies. METHODSParticipants underwent A{beta} PET imaging and plasma pTau217 measurement on up to three assay platforms across three cohorts. We then developed conversion equations using Deming regression - collectively named Biomarker Convert - and evaluated robustness using independent research cohorts. Finally, we modeled the potential impact of pTau217 screening on trial enrollment. RESULTSWhile absolute plasma pTau217 concentrations differed, the assays had similar predictive characteristics for A{beta} positivity (LC-MS/MS [C2N], AUC=0.952; Janssen Simoa, AUC=0.946; Lumipulse, AUC=0.929). Biomarker Convert enabled transformation of plasma pTau217 data across assays independent of A{beta} PET and clinical status. Plasma pTau217 reduced A{beta} PET scans in the model screening paradigm by >60%. DISCUSSIONBiomarker Convert equations enable harmonization of plasma pTau217 values from immunoassay and mass spectrometry platforms, supporting direct data comparison.

infographic.key_insight: Biomarker Convert is a computational method that harmonizes plasma pTau217 measurements across immunoassay and mass spectrometry platforms so results can be directly compared.
infographic.clinical_relevance: By standardizing pTau217 readouts, the tool could simplify biomarker screening and reduce the need for Aβ PET scans when identifying participants for Alzheimer’s research trials.
method: Measured plasma pTau217 across up to three assay platforms in three cohorts
Built cross-platform conversion equations using Deming regression
Tested robustness in independent research cohorts and modeled trial-screening impact
infographic.evidence_signal: Across platforms, pTau217 showed similarly strong Aβ-positive prediction (AUC 0.929-0.952), and the screening model suggested >60% fewer Aβ PET scans could be needed.
infographic.watch_item: Conversion equations need careful validation before routine use because assay performance, cohort makeup, and platform calibration can vary across sites.
infographic.paper_title: Biomarker Convert: a novel approach to transform plasma pTau217 results across immunoassay and mass spectrometry analytical platforms

title: Methylation-associated Gene Expression (MaGE): a non-invasive, in vivo measure of cellular senescence.
authors: Simpson, D. J.; Crofts, S. J.; Mavrommatis, C.; White, T. A.; Suwanlikit, Y. J.; Loyva, K.; Rocca, W. A.; Kantarci, K.; Mielke, M.; Richmond, A.; Marioni, R. E.; Kirschner, K.; LeBrasseur, N. K.; Chandra, T.
abstract: Cellular senescence is a central hallmark of aging, yet its measurement in humans remains invasive, low-throughput and tissue-specific, precluding population-scale study. We developed Methylation-associated Gene Expression (MaGE) predictors: whole-blood DNA methylation proxies of p14ARF, p16INK4A and p21CIP1 expression, plus a composite score, providing the first scalable measure of senescence-marker expression. Deployed across Generation Scotland (n=18,859), MaGE yielded 45 Bonferroni-significant associations spanning 18 incident diseases and all-cause mortality. The two strongest associations recapitulated the established tissue specificity of p21CIP1 and p16INK4A activation, with MaGE-p21 associating with incident alcoholic liver disease and MaGE-p16 with pulmonary fibrosis. In a separate study, MaGE tracked disease severity and treatment response in Crohns disease. MaGE is a scalable, interpretable biomarker of senescence that enables its study at population scale and offers a route to patient stratification in senolytic trials.

infographic.key_insight: MaGE uses whole-blood DNA methylation to estimate senescence-marker gene expression, creating a scalable proxy for cellular senescence in humans.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help stratify patients and support population-scale studies or senolytic trial design by linking senescence signals to disease risk and severity.
method: Built methylation-based predictors for p14ARF, p16INK4A, p21CIP1, and a composite score.
Applied the proxies to large human cohorts to test links with incident disease and mortality.
Validated disease-specific signals, including associations with pulmonary fibrosis, alcoholic liver disease, and Crohn’s disease severity/treatment response.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Generation Scotland (n=18,859), MaGE showed 45 Bonferroni-significant associations across 18 incident diseases and all-cause mortality.
infographic.watch_item: Because MaGE is derived from whole blood, tissue specificity and downstream clinical interpretation may be limited for diseases driven by other organs.
infographic.paper_title: Methylation-associated Gene Expression (MaGE): a non-invasive, in vivo measure of cellular senescence.
